projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Don Egolf was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Give me your name.

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: I'm Don Egolf. Presently a resident here at the Old Soldiers Home, and my career as a soldier, I was in the U.S. Army and I started my career on 19 July, 1944, where I went to basic training at Fort Blanding, Florida.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Were you drafted, Don?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: No, I was not drafted. I enlisted. I never was drafted in my whole 20 years in the Army. I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Where did you enlist? What town were you in when you enlisted?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Was that your hometown?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: No, my hometown was Royersford, about 35 miles west of Philadelphia and I was inducted right there in Philadelphia at the Armory on Broad Street.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Was there quite a few people from your hometown?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: There were four of us.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Four of you?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yes, that went from Draft Board, yes.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Wow. Ok. So then you went to boot and where did you go after you were sworn-in?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: After I was sworn-in I went to Cumberland, Pennsylvania, that is near Harrisburg, that is where we got our uniforms, were issued our uniforms and two days later we hopped on a train and ended up in Florida, Camp Blanding, Florida, where we had four -- I beg your pardon, where we had 17 weeks' of basic training and after that we went home for a week and from there we went on to Camp Shanks in New York, where they put us on a boat to ship to Germany, well to France. We got off at France and hopped on a 40x8 and from there we went into Heerlen, Holland and into there, we went into Germany into combat.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: So you had 17 weeks?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: 17 weeks and that was in December. By January we were well into combat.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Let's go back to your basic training. Did you -- was it a culture shock for you to go into basic? You weren't very old; You were a young boy

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: I was 24 years old when I went into basic training and yes, it was a shock. But they kept us so busy, and 11-, 12-, 13-hour days were nothing and it was seven weeks before we even got a pass to go into town from Starke into St. Augustine is where my first pass was in Florida. And I tell you, we worked hard in basic. I will tell you that was an experience right then and there.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: You learned a lot of discipline?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yes, strict discipline and learning weapons and learning how to conduct yourself in combat, and exactly how to take care of yourself, and --

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Did you feel that basic training was a good experience for going into battle?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes, I did. They didn't think it was, but yes, you learned your weapon, you learned your weapon well, the M-1 Grand Rifle. You learned a lot of discipline, and you learned it in large numbers, which is good. From that you learn the buddy-system, how you worked together not only in combat, but in real-life, which was real good, I thought.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Tell me when you arrived in a foreign country, what happened then?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: What happened then, like I said, we got off the ship, and it was raining, of course. And we went about, I'd say about 200 yards, we walked 200 yards, and hopped on the train, which they called 40x8s, that is the size of the cars we got in. They were cars that transported us to -- I don't know how many were in them in one car, but the shipload got on a train, I'd say about half a mile long and from there we went into Reims, France, where they let us off for a while to look around and do a few things. And from there, we went on to I believe it was Heerlen, Holland, where we were briefed about combat, and so forth, and where we slept in this building on the floor, bare floor. I don't think anybody got any sleep, but the next morning --

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: You slept on the floor?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yes, we slept on the floor. There were no pillows, no blankets, no mattresses, no nothing. But I think they were getting us ready for foxholes is what they were doing. From there we went to our companies. I was assigned to E-Company. 405th Infantry, 102nd Division and I remember going into a -- they were already bivouacked in a bombed-out house, but they did have a kitchen setup where they fed us and get us ready for combat, which was -- I can't think of the name of the City -- but that next morning, we trekked to the Roer River, where we were set up in another bombed-out house and got ready for the Roer River crossing, of which I wrote a story about. We were there approximately days waiting for the Roer River to recede because prior to that the Germans bombed out the dam, way up, and it was flooded and it was impossible to cross for that reason. But I'd say a week, eight days later, we did cross and that was on February the 23rd, 1944.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Let's go back just for history sake and talk about the detail. When you say they fed you in this bombed-out house, what kind of food? Was that rations or what?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: No, they made coffee, which everybody wanted, but they had dehydrated eggs. They had dehydrated meat, and they had -- there was no fresh fruit, no bread or anything like that. They had a hard biscuit. They had a chocolate bar, I remember, for dessert, but the food that they cooked in the Mess Hall was something else.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: How many men were with you then?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: How many men in our company? I'd say there's about oh, maybe 70-80 personnel in Easy Company at that time.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Let's go on then to the river, that sounds interesting. You waited for the flood to recede.

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: While waiting for that we had to go back into Belgium to a river, about the same size as the Roer and there were Ducks. They were called Ducks, a type of land and water transportation, and we trained in those. Although they were never used, that's what we trained in. The whole time we were waiting and I said before we had our Mess Hall with us, I mean our kitchen with us, and get some food at times. Most were K-rations. The K-rations had four cigarettes in it, two Chiclets, a chocolate bar, toilet tissue. We were pretty well-prepared and, of course, we didn't get much sleep, not with about 35 of us in the cellar of a bombed-out house.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Were you still sleeping on the floor?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yes, cellar floor, yes. Oh, yeah, that's combat for you. That's the way it goes.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: That's what we want to know. So were you scared, or the adrenalin?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: What's scared? You are not afraid of what you don't know anything about, but you have an idea what is going to happen. And yes, you do have fear of that. Yes. That is the way it is in combat. You are not scared of what you don't know anything about, but you have an idea what is going to happen, and yes, you do have fear of that. Yes, that is the way it is in combat. After you get into combat and they start shooting at you, you lose all of that. Combat is very exciting, very, very exciting and as long as you are still living, it's more exciting. But then when you get hit, you lose all that.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Tell me what happened when you crossed the river? Was it light or dark?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: 3 o'clock in the morning -- 3 o'clock in the morning, our artillery opened up and there was a barrage of artillery approximately three-quarters of an hour of that and we went down through the river and down at the river bottom, or at the banks, it was these boats with an engineer in it to do the steering. And six men got in the boat, three on each side, and they were given orders and we rowed over to the other side. The engineer was in the back steering us. And as I wrote in my story, when we got to the other side, out of the nose -- the front part of our boat got stuck in the mud in the front, and the engineer was trying to bring it around, so we could get out of the sides -- the side of the boat. But he couldn't do it. So I thought I would help him and I started pushing and I pushed him and he fell over into the icy water. I have that in my story

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Did he survive?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: I don't know. Oh, hey, we had to rush out -- excuse me, we had to rush out of the boats and go and I had what they called the demolition-type of piece that the engineers might have to use on the other side. I carried that over and as soon as I got to the other side, I got rid of that. It was a heavy piece of detonation-type piece and I got rid of that. From there we went on and came to a ditch, a ditch about 3' deep. At the top it was about 3' wide. It was -- knowing the good times it was a waterway for them to water their crops, but there was about 1' wide water in the bottom and it was about maybe 6 or 7" deep. We had to cross that and there was no way of crossing that and keeping one foot dry. So what you did, you jumped in with one foot and hurdled over the top. From there we went on and, ironically, we got separated. We came into what they call a Pincer's movement, where we came in together like this, and firing on each other with nobody got -- nobody got hurt. We recognized each other and we went on to the City of Tetz.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: So that is a good thing you were bad shots, huh? [laughter ]

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. That was the beginning of combat for quite a few, but there were seasoned men there also. Yes, nobody got hit, that was good. And from Tetz, we went on from there.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Is that in Germany? Is Tetz in Germany?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yes, Tetz. Yes, it was on the other side of the Roer River. Our mission was to cross the Roer River and go onto the Rhine. That was our mission and, well, that's what happened the first night, the first night out, as I wrote in the story, we were dug-in, and we had two men to a foxhole, and what we did was, we tried -- one man would try to get some sleep, while the other guy stood guard. At this present time, as I wrote in the story, I was looking towards the east, and there was two towns on fire, and between these two fires, I saw a silhouette of a man coming toward me. Remember now we were on the frontline, and this man come towards me and I challenged him. He didn't say anything, and so I challenged him again, and so I, with my Browning Automatic Rifle, I fired one shot and I hit one of our own men in the neck. It was just right in here. It was a million-dollar wound. But just think if I would have opened up with that automatic weapon, I would have cut his head off, you know what I mean?

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: He didn't hear your challenges, I suppose, huh?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Well, he did, but he wasn't the enemy. He was one of our own men, so he didn't answer.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: What happened after that?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Well, the next day we went on to -- I can't remember the town names, but we went on and you must remember after the Roer River things were getting better for our troops, because they were running out of gasoline. Their troops were thinning. Their tanks were not running, because of lack of gasoline, and things were looking a lot better for us. So we went pretty fast, and by night, well, what we did was we would find a place to -- well, I won't use the word "bivouac" but we used homes to stay in. Whereby we didn't know the families, or the troops that just left or what? But they all retreated, leaving their homes and we were given their homes, and tried to get some rest for a few hours before we went on, and that was at night. Then the next day we'd go on again and we would find the enemy, and there was no retreating of any type during this mission, and eventually we went on until we did come to the Rhine. I can remember Monchengladbach, which was an airport just outside of Krefeld, Germany and the steel mill was there, too. And I remember we had a hard time there getting into that town. But after we got into that town, we found -- we learned that the enemy had crossed the Roer River and they were retreating very fast at that time.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Were you being shot at?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yeah, the enemy was there to shoot at us. Oh, yeah, but it wasn't like in France, along the hedgerows, or anything like that. That was the hard part, the hedgerows in France, yeah.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Would you like some more?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: No, that's okay.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: When you got to the Rhine River, what happened?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: When we got to the Rhine River, we halted. And after Intelligence found out that the troops on the other side were a bit disorganized without gasoline, without engines -- I mean without gasoline -- not completely without, but very short on gasoline, short on supplies, short on food, and short on all of these things. They thought if they were to have counterattacked on us, that we should the 70 -- we posed as the 79th division, with grown-up rubber tanks and trucks and recorded noises of engines running and things like this, and evidently it worked. But three days after that, we went across the Rhine, after Remagen Bridge was found intact and then we went on and things were not half as difficult as they were before, because of that -- they were really retreating at that time.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: How far did you --

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: We were on our way to Berlin, but we stopped at the Rhine at Tangermunde. That is where Arrow E Company was stopped, Tangermunde Bridge and at that time the Polish Army and the Russians were driving elements of the German Army this way, towards us from east to west, and we were taking German prisoners. They had no weapons. They dropped their weapons and asked are you going to fight the Germans? Are you going to fight the Polish? I said no, they are not the enemy; you're the only enemy. It was very interesting, but we took hundreds and hundreds of prisoners, in three or four days. Then as things settled down, then they got volleyballs to us, nets and things like this. It was very difficult to keep troops pacified if they are not fighting. So that is what they did. They brought us volleyballs and baseball bats and gloves and that's what we did all day long, waiting to see what -- well, they said that they expected the truce in just a few days. That's what we did while we were waiting for that, which was what? May 8th, '45.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Was the __+ River where the Russians - the Americans meshed with the Russians?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yes. Yes, in fact, I have pictures of the Russians and our boys, but we were restricted from going across to meeting these people, but we did anyway. We went over and took pictures, you know? And we talked as much German as we knew and what they knew and we were able to get a few words across that we understood each other and they were very young. We knew their rank and we talked about their rank and everything and their traveling coming this way, but they were not troops like us. They were very barbaric -- well, I won't go into that.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Well, do. I mean, it's part of your life.

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: You can imagine what they did to the women and when they were finished they just killed them.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: They just killed them?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yes. Yes, they did that and when they went into a town they just cleaned it out. And we heard stories where they wanted to remove a toilet tank and take it from the wall and take it home. Things like this -- things like -- we heard all kind of stories.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: So with Peace being declared?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Everybody wants to go home. Everybody wants to go home. Well, like I say, they kept us busy, which is best thing you could do, and they moved us around at least every two weeks and it was the best thing that happened for morale. You'd be surprised; we recognized that. And we found cars and if we could get gas, we drove their cars around . We did things like this, you know? And then at that time we were in countries. We weren't in cities. In the country you found families that stayed in their farms, you know? There was some fraternization, which was not allowed at that time. But there was fraternization and we would go and look at gardens and things like this, and we'd see plots where they buried stuff, you know? And we'd dig it up and there would be fresh vegetables. They had it out in the country. They didn't have it in the city and we would see that it was all divided up into the small towns and to make sure that the kids got it. I shouldn't be telling you this, I guess. That's the way it was.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: How long were you there?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: I came home and I got home January the 6th, '46. I had two daughters, which were 24 points apiece. I wasn't one of the first ones, but I was the next group out, yes. We moved over to France, to Camp Lucky Strike, and we had a little time there. That's where I buried seven weapons that I had in my bag and they said -- they told us if you get on the ship with any guns, we're going to send you back into combat. That's what they used So I threw those seven -- I had Lugers and all kinds

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: That was incentive, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Then what did you do?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: I think it was -- oh, while there "Porgy and Bess," an all-black troop put on "Porgy and Bess." And the first night hardly anybody went, but when they heard how good the show was, the next night, I tell you, when they opened the doors the crowd in front just kept pushing and pushing and there at the door, brass buttons from the coats, you know? The overcoats. Piles of them, at the doorway there. That was the strangest thing. And a couple of guys were pushed up over the crowd, because they were about to pass out, you know? They were grouped -- it was something else.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Oh, wow!

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: That was something else, but I think about a week later we got on a ship and -- a victory ship and came on back

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Where did you dock?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: I did bring a P-38 home with me.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Oh, did you?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yeah and I showed it to a guy in Camp Shanks -- I believe was Camp Shanks. Anyway, I showed him this P-38 and he said. I'll give you 35 bucks for that. I said, give it to me. I didn't have no money. I said, I'll take it. But they are worth a lot of money now, the P-38s.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: What did you do then?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Well, then we processed. We went to Personnel and we processed and they gave us some money and , boy, we went to the cafeteria and ate ice cream, and drank milk, and cake [Laughter ]

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: What did do you in your career after that? You got out of service?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yes, I got out. I went right through Pennsylvania, but I went there and I processed, and in three days I was gone.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: What did you do?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Anyway, what is the name of that? What I did was -- well, I went home to my family. I had my wife and two girls and I got a job with a tree company. I put in for the GI Bill and went into an apprenticeship with this tree company, and Uncle Sam paid most of my salary. They paid some. And it was within a little over a year and I just got the bug, which I did -- nobody could understand why, but it's just something that hit me and I stayed for 20 years.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: What did do you in that 20 years? What were you doing?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: What was I doing? Well, the first thing I did was I went to the Police Academy at Carlisle Barracks in Pennsylvania. And I learned I got orders - well, I was on orders to go to Panama, but for some reason that was rescinded and I got orders for Korea. This was 1947. Korea was nothing then. The Japanese, had just left a couple of years ago and they had nothing. Our U.S. Government was moving in to take over, and help them at that time. Yeah, I was at the Replacement Depot in Suwon, Korea and there I was Security. Well, the biggest thing for us to do was to keep the Koreans out from coming in and stealing. And at that time, when one of them did come in and steal anything, well, I shouldn't be telling this.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: It's fine. It's your story.

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: At that time in 1947 we shot them and killed them and called the CID to come on in and investigate. And they did and that was the end of it. But six months into that, our U.S. Military Government was in, and they took over, which was the right thing to do. We processed people in and we processed people out, coming into Korea and leaving Korea.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Meaning military?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yes, military. Yes, our own U.S. Army.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: How long were you in Korea?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: One year, just one year. The second time I was in Korea, I was in there about 14-and-a-half months.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: That was during the War?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: It was after the Korean War, '63.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: After Korea, the first time?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: After that, well, I went to Japan and then I put in for my wife and kids and they came over and we lived in Rokko Heights, which was in Kobe, Japan. And I was in the Military Police there

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Did you enjoy Japan?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes. The Japanese People, they're a family people, a nice people. They are progressive. We couldn't say that about the Koreans, because they didn't have nothing to progress with, you know? But no, the Japanese were wonderful people. They're family people.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: How long were you in Japan?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: About four-and-a-half years. When the Korean War started, we were there for a while. But I was on orders to go home, and take my family with me, but they said hey, you take your family to the POE, to the Port, and you come back. You don't go with them. And I came back and that is when I became an investigator for the Provost Marshal, which was very interesting. About two years, I guess.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: In Japan?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: In Japan. I even signed up to go to Korea, so I could go home quicker, but the Personnel Officer was a friend of mine and said you are not going to Korea while I'm here. [laughter ]

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: So after Japan, you came back; right?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yes, I came back to the States. Yes. Where did I go from there? Yes, Security and Intelligence. That was balance of my career.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: With all the clearances and everything?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Yes, I can't remember the year, but I had a good assignment, from the second time in Korea, I came to Fort Carson. I was assigned to the 5th Military Intelligence as Sergeant, which was interesting. I was there for almost two years and they started taking my people over to Vietnam. I was losing people, and those people were not sending money to their wives and wives were telling me they didn't have money to buy their babies food. I would like to have the money back -- well, I didn't loan it out. I gave it to them.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Did you go on to Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: When did you get out of the Service?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: 1 May, 1966, I left the service. And what I did was I went to California for a while and then I went to the Red Cross, and signed up with them. I went to the school in Fort Ord, California, which was very interesting. And then I was assigned to Camp Pendleton, which is a Marine base down there, which was very interesting, as an Assistant Field Director. Well, what did I do then? My family and I moved down there and I was there for a couple of years. What am I trying to say -- Assistant Field Director, yes. Yes, there at Camp Pendleton that is a Marine base and you had people that came into the Marines that were not fit to be Marines, you know what I mean? They were not gung-ho and they would come to us and they would want to get out and would want this and want that and we would tell them any emergencies must be activated at the hometown. You cannot activate anything here to get out of the Marines. And those kids that didn't want to be Marines. They were sad cases. It was terrible. But we tried helping them, as much as we can. We'd get calls from the wives, my husband isn't sending me any money and I don't have money to feed my babies and we'd give them money. Those are the kind of things that you did.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Did you retire them from the Red Cross?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: No, I was asked, after about a year-and-a-half there, I was to go on orders to go to Vietnam, which was in the summertime. And I didn't feel I was physically able to do that, so I got out of the Red Cross, for that purpose. Del Mar, California and on the beach for a while, and went to New Port Beach, and I asked them to take me on as an arborist, is what I learned when I came back from combat. I was there working in the tree work, so I couldn't make more money. So I quit that and went out and bought a pickup and put a lift on it and I went into business for myself, doing tree work in New Port Beach. I did for a year-and-a-half when I was trying to dig out a stump one day and I hurt my back and that was the end of that. What did I do after that? Nothing, I guess. 32 years with the VA in Long Beach, California, where they treated me royally. But I heard about this place and about the facilities surrounding it, the medical facilities and so forth and I was having problems at the time that I thought that maybe I could do better with here at the Old Soldiers Home. And I applied for it and they told me to come on in and I now I like it very much. It is a good place to be for somebody that has physical problems, and not only that, there is a lot of things here that are very good to get with the trips and the Mess Hall is exceptional, I think. Some people don't, but I think it's exceptional, very good. And they do what they can for you, even though there is a program on now to save money, which interferes with some things. But it is still a fine place to be, even though there are only two federal -- two federal facilities like this in the country, there are also this type of facilities in each state, which I understand are okay. But not half as good as what we have here, if I may say so?

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Don, let me ask you --?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: No, I was married and I had two kids, but it's just something that I felt, something that I had to do. I wasn't drafted. I went to the Draft Board -- what I told them, I said I would like to go into Service, but I would like to be in the Navy. If I sign up, will you put me in the Navy? Oh, yeah, we'll put you in the Navy. The next day I ended up in the Army, which I was very happy that I was. After riding the Atlantic in a victory ship, I was glad I wasn't in the Navy, and also crossing the English Channel, I got sick- [laughter ] Yes, would I do it again? Yes, yes I would. And I have a big Flag picture in my room which I look at quite often and say yes, I would do it again. And of course, I'm in a room where I can look out the window and see our Flag out in the-- [laughter ]

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: It made you well?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yes, in combat there are no questions, no questions. Answers -- immediately, if not sooner, but in combat -- well, you're beside -- you're never separated in combat. Only when you might become a big target, but the friendship and the compatibility is what I'm trying to say. The compatibility is 100% and you are always looking out for the other guy. You don't think of yourself. That is the way combat is.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: It was definitely a band of brothers?

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Yes, the compatibility with everybody is the same. There was a time I thought there was a young Lieutenant, he was a little too eager than he should have been and he wanted to attack all the time. Well, you only attack when you learn what your Intelligence has found out about the enemy. Before you attack and go into the enemy, you have to find out what it's all about first. I didn't think of that, but no, the Officers and they are very careful. They are very thoughtful before they do anything. And they gave orders and that is what you do.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: So unless --

sp.speaker: Don Egolf
sp.p: Only something you can understand if you are in it. You can't ever tell somebody about combat, that is impossible. Well, I think they are, yes.

sp.speaker: Donna Steiger
sp.p: Thank you.
